Empirical Research Plan  

------------------------------------------------------------  
1. Identification Strategy  
------------------------------------------------------------  
Preferred strategy: Difference-in-Differences (DID) combined with an event-study and an IV extension.

Why DID?  
• The 1981-82 recession generated a discrete, plausibly exogenous shock to TSPs that differed sharply across counties depending on ex-ante industrial intensity.  
• We observe the same counties for several years before (1978-80) and after (1983-84) the shock, allowing us to difference out time-invariant county characteristics with county fixed effects and common macro trends with year fixed effects.  
• An event-study version lets us (i) test the parallel-trends assumption and (ii) trace dynamics that separate fetal from post-natal exposure.  

Why add an IV?  
Even after differencing, residual endogeneity may remain if economic downturns directly affect infant health. We will instrument the continuous change in TSPs with ( initial 1977 pollution-intensive employment share × national recession dummy ), i.e., a Bartik‐style shock that captures county-specific exposure to the national collapse in steel and other smokestack industries but is orthogonal to local infant-health shocks except through emissions.

------------------------------------------------------------  
2. Treatment and Control  
------------------------------------------------------------  
Treatment variable  
Main continuous treatment: ΔTSP_{ct} = log(TSP level_{ct}). For nonlinear estimates we will also use indicators for TSP > 75 µg/m³ and for TSP decile bins.

Binary treatment (for DID graphs): counties whose pre-recession TSP trend-adjusted level was in the top quartile AND that had ≥10 % of 1977 employment in SIC 33 (primary metals) or SIC 34–37 (fabricated metals, machinery, transport eqpt.) are “high-exposed”.

Control group  
Counties below median TSP and with <5 % employment in pollution-intensive SICs, not adjacent to high-exposed counties.

Treatment timing  
Post = 1982–1984 (first full calendar year after the recession; 1981 can be included as “placebo post-1”).  

Event date = 1981:Q4 NBER business-cycle peak. In the event-study we code dummies for t = −3,…,+3 relative to 1982.

IV first stage  
Z_{ct} = InitialSteelShare_c × Post_t  

------------------------------------------------------------  
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Parallel pre-trends: In absence of the recession-induced pollution drop, infant outcomes in treated and control counties would have continued to evolve similarly.  
Plausibility: Pre-recession health and economic aggregates moved in parallel; this will be visually and statistically tested in the event-study using 1978–80.

A2. Shock exogeneity conditional on FE and covariates: The size of the TSP decline is driven by industrial composition, not by county-specific contemporaneous shocks that also affect infant health (e.g., local health-care cuts).  
Plausibility: The recession’s demand collapse for steel was national, and plant shutdowns were predominantly permanent because of the 1977 CAAA rules, not county policy.

A3. No major migration/selection of births correlated with treatment.  
Plausibility: Infant-health–relevant migration over a two-year window is limited; we will test for changes in number of births and parental SES.

A4. Stable unit treatment value (no spillovers) at the county level.  
Plausibility: Some cross-boundary pollution spillovers exist; adjacency exclusions for the control group and robustness to including down-wind neighbors mitigate this.

------------------------------------------------------------  
4. Threats to Identification & Remedies  
------------------------------------------------------------  
T1. Economic downturn directly harms infant health (income, stress, health-care cuts).  
Remedy: (i) Include county×year unemployment and BEA income controls; (ii) control for transfer payments (AFDC, Medicaid, etc.); (iii) IV that isolates only the manufacturing-based pollution component.

T2. Measurement error in TSPs because monitors are not uniformly distributed.  
Remedy: Weight counties by number of monitors; instrument ΔTSP with the Bartik shock; run robustness restricting to counties with ≥2 monitors and to monitors <2 km from population centers.

T3. Differential pre-existing trends in health care access or demographic composition.  
Remedy: Add county-specific linear trends; include time-varying controls for number of physicians per 1,000 residents, hospital beds, and demographic structure from County & City Data Book.

------------------------------------------------------------  
5. R Code Outline  
------------------------------------------------------------  
```r
# -------------- 0. Packages ------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dim FE and IV
library(did)         # event study (Callaway–Sant’Anna)
library(stargazer)

# -------------- 1. Load Data ------------------
birth   <- fread("birth_county_year.csv")      # births by county-year-race-gender
death   <- fread("infant_deaths_county_year.csv")
tsp     <- fread("tsp_county_year.csv")
econ    <- fread("county_econ.csv")            # income, unemployment, transfers
indus   <- fread("county_industry_1977.csv")   # baseline SIC employment shares
weather <- fread("weather_county_year.csv")

# -------------- 2. Merge & Construct ---------
setkeyv(birth, c("county","year","race","gender"))
setkeyv(death, c("county","year","race","gender"))
panel <- merge(birth, death, all = TRUE)
panel <- merge(panel, tsp,    by = c("county","year"))
panel <- merge(panel, econ,   by = c("county","year"))
panel <- merge(panel, weather,by = c("county","year"))
panel <- merge(panel, indus,  by = "county")

# Infant mortality per 1,000 live births
panel[, imr := 1000 * (infant_deaths / live_births)]

# Main treatment: log TSP and its change
panel[, lntsp := log(tsp_mean)]
panel <- panel[order(county, year)]
panel[, dlntsp := lntsp - shift(lntsp), by = county]

# Bartik instrument
panel[, steel_share := steel_emp77/total_emp77]
panel[, post        := as.integer(year >= 1982)]
panel[, bartik      := steel_share * post]

# Define treated counties for DID graphs
panel[, treated := as.integer(steel_share > quantile(steel_share, .75))]

# -------------- 3. Main FE-DID Regressions ---
# 3.1 Simple DID: treated × post
did_spec <- feols(imr ~ treated*post + unem_rate + percap_income | county + year,
                  data = panel, weights = ~live_births)
summary(did_spec)

# 3.2 Continuous treatment with IV
iv_spec <- feols(imr ~ 1 | county + year | lntsp ~ bartik,
                 data = panel, weights = ~live_births, cluster = ~county)
summary(iv_spec)

# 3.3 Event study
es <- att_gt(yname = "imr",
             tname = "year",
             idname = "county",
             gname = "first_treat_year",   # compute from treated & post
             xformla = ~ unem_rate + percap_income,
             data = panel)
agg_es <- aggte(es, type = "dynamic")
summary(agg_es)
ggplot(agg_es$egt_long, aes(event.time, Estimate)) +
  geom_point() + geom_line() + theme_bw() + geom_vline(xintercept = -1, lty = 2)

# 3.4 Non-linearity: above/below 75 µg/m³
panel[, above75 := as.integer(tsp_mean > 75)]
nl_spec <- feols(imr ~ above75*post | county + year,
                 data = panel, weights = ~live_births)
summary(nl_spec)

# -------------- 4. Robustness Check -----------
# Exclude counties adjacent to treated
panel_adj <- panel[adjacent_to_treated==0]
iv_adj <- update(iv_spec, data = panel_adj)
etable(iv_spec, iv_adj, tex = FALSE)

```

------------------------------------------------------------  
6. Expected Results  
------------------------------------------------------------  
Direction: Higher particulate pollution increases infant mortality and worsens birth outcomes (lower birth weight, shorter gestation, lower 1-minute APGAR).  

Magnitude prior: A 10 µg/m³ decline in annual TSP is expected to reduce infant mortality by roughly 0.5 deaths per 1,000 live births (≈5–7 % of the 1980 mean of 9.2/1,000). Consistent with epidemiological estimates of 0.04–0.08 additional infant deaths per µg/m³.

Heterogeneity: Larger effects for Black infants and for males; threshold effects above the 75 µg/m³ standard; most of the effect likely operates through fetal exposure (gestation) rather than postnatal, so reductions should be largest for neonatal (<28 days) deaths.

------------------------------------------------------------  
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  
C1: Common pre-trends tested and satisfied visually/statistically ………………… 1  
C2: No simultaneous confounders (economic controls + IV) ………………………… 0.8  
C3: No treatment spillovers (adjacency robustness) ………………………………… 0.7  
C4: Stable composition (birth counts, parental SES stable) ………………………… 0.9  
C5: Correct functional form / standard errors clustered at county ……………… 1  
Overall ≈ 4.4 / 5 – reasonable but not bullet-proof.
